speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
when the house rose at six o'clock I was about to discuss the differences between the export and domestic freight rates as applied to certain grain movements. On shipments from North Battleford to Vancouver the export rate on wheat is 14-4 cents per bushel while the domestic rate is 30 cents; in other words, the export rate is 15-6 cents per bushel less than the domestic. On oats from the same point the export rate is 8-1 cents per bushel and the domestic rate, 17 cents per bushel, a difference of 8-9 cents per bushel. Following this shipment through to Shanghai and allowing for all intervening charges such as handling and ocean freight, it works out that the poultry feeder in Shanghai can secure our feed wheat for 4-85 cents per bushel less than the poultry feeder in British Columbia, and he can secure our oats for nearly 2 cents per bushel less. On shipments of barley from Areola the export rate is 13-92 cents per bushel and the domestic rate, 25-68 cents, a difference in favour of the export rate of 11-76 cents per bushel. Carrying this shipment of barley through to Shanghai it will be found that the Chinese feeder can secure barley for 2-8 cents per bushel less than the feeder in British Columbia.
Going the other way and taking shipments of grain from the bay ports, it will be found that the export rate is 7-7 cents iper bushel on barley and the domestic rate 19-9 cents, an advantage in favour of the export shipper of 12-2 cents. After allowing for all charges such as elevator charges and ocean freight, this barley can be delivered to feeders of live stock in Liverpool at 6.85 cents per bushel cheaper than it can be delivered to feeders in St. John. That seems to be too much of a discrepancy.
Looking at the question from another angle we find that at to-day's price No. 4 C.W. barley is worth 38 cents per bushel at Fort William. The freight rate from Souris, Manitoba, to Fort William is 8-16 cents. The local price at Souris less the elevator charges is 31-84 cents per bushel, and it costs 34-5 cents per bushel in freight and other handling charges to place the grain in the hands of the feeder in the maritimes. The feeder in the maritimes has to pay 31 cents per bushel plus 34-5 cents per bushel in handling charges,
making a total of 65 cents per bushel for the barley for which the farmer at Souris receives only 31 cents per bushel.
Let us now consider feed wheat shipped from Areola, Saskatchewan. At to-day's prices this wheat is worth 45 cents per bushel; the freight to Fort William is 11 cents per bushel, making a value of the grain art Areola, less elevator and handling charges, 33 cents per bushel. The domestic rate to Vancouver is 25-6 cents per bushel, and the Vancouver poultry feeder has to pay 33-5 cents per bushel plus 25-6 cents for freight, a total of 59-1 cents per bushel for feed wheat for which the farmer at Areola receives 33 cents. We are trying to establish live stock and poultry industries in Canada and yet we oblige the producers to pay these excessive freight rates. For the life of me I cannot understand a policy which gives a greater advantage to the feeder of bacon hogs in Denmark than is given to the feeder in eastern Canada. Likewise, I cannot understand why an advantage should be given to the poultry raiser in China over and above that given to the poultry raiser in British Columbia.
A few days ago the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Maophail), speaking on the resolution in connection with the bonus on wheat, said in effect that she would support the principle of paying a bonus .to the western farmer if it would keep him out of mixed farming. I should think it would be much more reasonable to adapt our freight rate structure so that an advantage could be given both ways. At the present time if the eastern farmer wants to buy our western feed grain he is obliged to pay more because of the domestic freight rate. If this rate was reduced by, say, five cents per bushel, it would mean that we could produce and deliver that barley at five cents per bushel less, and the advantage would work both ways.
Manitoba, which is one of the older grain producing provinces, is particularly interested in the domestic freight rate structure. On account of the invasion of weeds and the running out of land the farmer in Manitoba has been forced into the growing of coarse grains, and as time goes on he will be compelled to grow a still larger percentage of this class of feed. I think it is only fair to state that Manitoba did not secure the same proportion of the five cent bonus on wheat as did the other western provinces, and consequently we are more interested directly in the reduction of domestic freight rates. More live stock should be fattened in eastern Canada with western grain and the poultry producer of British Columbia should be given an op-
Western Freight Rates

portundty to produce more of the country's requirements. The climatic conditions alone are sufficient to justify that contention. If these men were given the opportunity of securing our western feed grains at a reasonable rate, I think it would work out to the advantage of all concerned, the railways included.
I cannot understand why we should have a domestic freight rate structure which leaves us in our present position. The poultry raiser in British Columbia has to pay 4.85 cents per bushel more for wheat than does the poultry producer in China; he has to pay 2.8 cents per bushel more for barley and 1.99 cent per bushel more for oats. On an average the European feeder can secure his grains from Canada at 6.85 cents per bushel less than the eastern Canada feeder. Surely this works an injustice and is something that should be rectified in the very near future.
I am very glad that this subject has again been brought to the attention of the house, and I hope that this time some definite action will be taken in respect to it. We are particularly interested in the matter at this time because of the very severe crop conditions which we have had in practically all the western provinces; consequently we do feel that we have an added right to ask for some sort of adjustment in this regard. I therefore have very much pleasure in supporting the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) :
subtopic: REDUCTION OF DOMESTIC RATES ON GRAIN AND GRAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened most of the afternoon to the debate which has taken place on this question, and it has been a most interesting debate from every standpoint, a debate which I think showed moderation and fairness to a large extent, if not completely. Perhaps in a sense, though I do this with no controversial desire, I might except my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), because he seemed to think it very fair that the late government had done nothing for three years after the decision had been given in this case by the Board of Railway Commissioners, either to change that decision or to refer it back to the board, yet he seemed to think it most unfair that this government in less than one year and a half in power should not have settled the whole question. I think that this government has had very much more difficult and serious questions on its hands than had the late government during at least the last three years of its regime, and I think that the government of to-day has had a good deal of reason for being hesitant in undertaking more heavy responsibilities. I should like generally though 
to compliment all the speakers, particularly the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) who introduced the resolution, and members on both sides of the house by and large, because generally speaking they spoke in a very moderate tone and I believe from their own standpoint were speaking as fairly as any of us would desire them to do.
It seems to me that there were two questions involved in the discussion which followed the resolution. The resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the domestic freight rate on grain and grain products moving from any point in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia, to a point in any of the said provinces, or from one point to another point in any one of the said provinces, be substantially reduced.
I think the word "should" ought to have been placed in the resolution. At any rate it is a very general resolution, but my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi and the other members from British Columbia on both sides of the house who addressed themselves to the question were speaking largely from the British Columbia standpoint, and so I say that there were two distinct questions involved in the discussion. There was first the question as to the domestic and export rate on grain to British Columbia, and secondly there was the question of freight rates on grain in general throughout the four western provinces. They are two questions quite distinct, and it was not on the latter question that there was an appeal to the late government from the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The appeal was on the first question, that of domestic and export rates on grain to British Columbia.
May I say at the outset that I sympathize very sincerely with my hon. friends from all parts of the western provinces who were speaking on behalf of the grain growers of those sections, because no one realizes more keenly than the government the serious plight in which the grain growers of the west find themselves. We all realize that they have been very badly hit. The prices of their commodities have gone down to perhaps one-third of what they were a few years ago, and consequently a reduction of one cent a bushel in freight rates is of very great importance to them. On the other hand, the two great railways of this country, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, as everybody in this house knows, have also been very hard hit, and while I do not wish to be construed as opposing the resolution-because I do not feel that I am capable any more than this house in general is capable of passing

Western Freight Rates
judicially on the merits of the case-at the same time I feel it my duty as Minister of Railways to point out to the house some of the difficulties of the question. After all, as Minister of Railways I am speaking for the government, but on the other hand, the railways themselves have no representation in the house to express their side of the question, and I feel that in fairness to them I ought to give a few of the arguments, whether I agree with them or not, which the railways put forward on their side. In other words, I am pointing out that there are two sides to this question, and that probably the truth lies in between the two, as it usually does with most questions. Fairness demands, however, that I offer a few of the reasons given by the railways why they do not agree at once to what looks on the face of it to be a very fair demand.
Export rates not only on grain but on all commodities are usually lower in all countries than domestic rates. They are lower because of the advantage which they give to producers and traders in a country to compete with traders in other countries on what somebody has expressed as a free trade basis. They give them an opportunity to compete in outside markets. Our export rates on grain are lower than our domestic rates, but so are our export rates on practically all other commodities. I do not wish to take up time by quoting rates on too many commodities, but I have a statement under my hand of the export rates on very many commodities and in practically every case they are very much lower than the domestic rates. For example, the domestic rate on apples per 100 pounds in carload lots to Halifax is 58 cents, and the export rate is 39i cents; on automobiles the domestic rate is 119 as opposed to 74; copper, 77J as opposed to 55; iron and steel, 35 as opposed to 22; newsprint paper, 19i as opposed to 15; packing house products, 114 as opposed to 93. I pick those out at random merely to illustrate the point which the railways make, that the export rates are lower not only on grain but also on all commodities for the reasons I have just given.
Yet at the same time one feels a good deal of sympathy with the arguments that have been put forward by various speakers in the house this afternoon, because it does not on the face of it seem fair that the export rate on grain, for instance, from Edmonton to Vancouver is 20 cents and the rate from Vancouver to the orient 18i cents, making a total from Edmonton to the orient of 38i cents, whereas the domestic rate from Edmonton to Vancouver is 41i cents, or a difference
of 3 cents in favour of the orient. I agree that that does not seem reasonable. On the other hand, some speakers have pointed out that they could ship grain more cheaply, so far as rates are concerned, to Denmark and Great Britain than, for example, to Vancouver.

With the exception of Mr. Oliver, who gave a dissenting judgment, the judgment of the railway commissioners was that "no justification could be

At any rate, the late government did hear the case on October 15, 16 and 17. I have no record before me to the effect that the hearing was adjourned, but I do not question the remarks of my hon. friend. However if the government heard the case finally' in January, 1930, they had six or seven months in which to give their decision, and yet they' gave none. I merely point that out as an historical fact showing that no doubt the late government were in the same position as we are-simply somewhat confused about the merits of the case.
Since we came into power I have on many occasions had this case before me. I sympathize with the statements made by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house concerning what would appear to be an unfair condition whereby domestic rates are higher than export rates. I have discussed that question with the heads of the two great transcontinental railway companies in Canada, and have been in conference with men in their traffic departments. I remember on one occasion having an interview with Mr. Stephens of the Canadian Pacific Railway Traffic Department and Mr. Burnap of the Canadian National Railways Traffic Department. Those two gentlemen were in my office regarding this question for an hour or longer on one occasion, and at that time I took the attitude which has been taken by many hon. members to-day to the effect that they might well throw off something from the domestic 
rate, thereby bringing it into closer alignment with the export rate. I argued that they might build up traffic which does not to-day exist and thereby add business to the railway companies. That was my feeling at that time, and speaking personally I cannot say that I have changed my views. Their reply however was that the export rate is not a fair one. They said, "We did not agree to the export rate; it was imposed upon us by the Board of Railway Commissioners." They claimed that it was a losing rate, and that in any event they could make no money from it. Further they said, "If you wish to approximate these rates the fair thing to do would be to raise the export rate, thereby bringing it closer to the domestic rate, rather than to lower the domestic rate." That is their argument and their side of the question.
They viewed the matter from another angle which I shall now outline. They said, "Suppose we agree to your suggestion"-may I add that the discussion was informal-" Suppose we agree to your suggestion, the next move would be that all the prairie provinces would demand the same lowering of rates we might give to British Columbia. Then would come the maritime provinces who in turn would demand a lowering of their rates. The result would be that a change in the freight rates in one section would promote applications to the railways from the whole country to bring rates into alignment with the lowered scale permitted in one section." There is a great deal of truth in that contention, and I think the discussion I have outlined shows that the railway companies have some grounds for the stand they have taken.
At this time I shall endeavour to give you some of the arguments they put before me, not necessarily in discussion but also by letter and on various occasions when the matter was under consideration. They claimed, first, that any change would affect the whole freight rates structure. Secondly, they said that if we applied the export rate on grain to British Columbia in connection with the domestic grain shipped to that province, and applied the same rate to grain shipped throughout the western provinces, the railways would suffer to the extent of nearly $2,000,000. They said the actual cost to them in 1930 would have been $1,680,000. They take the position that as the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway are not in a good financial condition at the present time they should not be asked to carry any greater load. We who have been following the railroad situation know that their statement of conditions is the correct one.

Further, they say that on the 20 cent export rate from Edmonton or Calgary, for instance, they are actually subsidizing export trade. They have figures to show that the railway companies are now subsidizing exports because they say on the 20 cent rate they are losing money. They pointed out to me that the Seattle export rate is from 31^ cents to 37-J cents as compared with the Canadian rate of 20 cents, the compared rates covering equal distances. In fact, they used those figures as an argument to show that they were giving much lower export rates than were given at Seattle, and that therefore they should be permitted to raise that rate.
They took the further stand-and I am attempting to give their arguments justly and fairly, not necessarily supporting them, because the house has a right to hear both sides of the question-that the Canadian rates on grain are the lowest in the world. They positively and absolutely make that statement, and have stated over and over again, and have presented evidence to prove-some of which I have in my hand-that in the United States the rates are higher for like distances.
For the information of hon. members I should like to review a few of the figures given to me to illustrate their point. From Brandon, Manitoba, to Fort William, a distance of 552 miles the export rate .per 100 pounds is 16 cents. From Boyle, North Dakota to Duluth, a distance of 553 miles, the rate is 27 cents. I ask hon. members to compare that with the 18 cents rate from Routledge to Fort William.

The railways give the comparative per ton mile rate for grain and other commodities, and they show that the rates on grain are less than half the rates on other commodities. Of course, that takes in package freight and all that sort of thing. Perhaps it is not a point of any great importance.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the railways claim that the rates are much lower in Canada than in the United States, and they feel that in view of their financial condition-and everybody here knows it to be somewhat serious-they should not be asked to absorb any greater loss than they are absorbing at the present time. May I point out, for example, that the Canadian National Railways for January and February have not been making their operating expenses. As they express it, they are "in the red," which is a very serious situation for any railway to be in. The other railway may not be in that condition, but it is also losing revenue heavily. The revenues of both roads have been going down very markedly this year even compared with last year. They claim, with some justification I think, that they should not be asked to take a further cut in freight rates without good cause. They point out that freight rates in the United States have not been lowered, but that on

Western Freight Rates
the contrary, recently the Interstate Commerce Commission granted increased rates on a number of commodities in an effort to put the railways of the United States in a better financial position.
There is one other point. An hon. member speaking to-day compared the export rate via British Columbia with the export rate from Fort William to Montreal and pointed out the differential was greater in the former case.
I do not question that at all. It must not be forgotten that the rate from Fort William to Montreal is kept down by water competition, and consequently is bound to be lower than the rate in a section where there is no water competition.
It does not seem to me, Mr. Speaker, nor do I think it does to my hon. friends who have argued this question, that either the government or the parliament of Canada is a rate making body. We have not the facilities to deal with such a complicated question. Surely the House of Commons has fewer facilities than has the government, because one side of the question has been presented here to-day, and unless I had chosen to give some of the arguments of the railways which they have passed on to me-and I have given them without necessarily claiming that they should be accepted-there would have been only one side of the question before the house. The House of Commons is not a rate making body, neither do I think the government of Canada is a rate making body. I remember reading a speech by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), in which he pointed out that it was doubtful if there should be an appeal to the governor in council from judgments of the railway commission with respect to freight rates. I think there is sound justification for that position. The Board of Railway Commissioners is a judicial body created for the purpose of dealing with freight rates. On the whole I think the railway commission is an excellent body. It gives its full time to questions of freight rates, and, generally speaking, it should be able to give reasonable satisfaction to the various sections of the country with respect to the general rate structure.
In view of this, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, who so eloquently presented his motion to the house, and those on both sides who have so ably supported him, should realize that they have explained their case very thoroughly to the government and that the government is seized of its importance. I think I can say to the house that within a reasonable time the appeal will be disposed of by the government in some way that at least will be fair with regard to the merits of the case. I can assure not only the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, but also the other hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house, who have taken a strong attitude on this question, that the government will give deep consideration to the matter, and I believe that as far as the government is concerned the question will be disposed of in the near future.

As my hon. friend the Minister of Railways said quite properly, there are two considerations which should be analysed in discussing this matter. I think the Minister of Railways is quite correct in stating that in the main domestic rates are higher in the United- States than they are in the Dominion of Canada, but

I believe my hon. friend will find that the differential between the domestic rate and the export rate is not as great in the United States. That is the specific complaint in British Columbia, that the differential between 20 cents and 41J cents is far too great. A government such as we have to-day, with its Canada first policy-I am not taiking politically, but rather in regard to the foundations of a tariff structure-surely should condemn a policy which makes it possible to export Canadian grain to China and Japan, permitting them to enter the $50,000,000 British market and sell their eggs at lower prices than the Canadian poultrymen. It seems to me there is something wrong.
I quite agree that there are two sides to this question; there is the larger, national side to it, and I am not unmindful of the fact that to-day in this country there is a large body of opinion holding the view that it is necessary, in order to maintain the vitality and the permanence of o,ur railways, that there should be a general increase in freight rates all over the country. I am somewhat affrighted lest the deliberations now under way in Canada in regard to our railway structure and our railway financial condition may imperil even the Crowsnest pass agreement, which has given great relief and opened up many avenues of progress to western Canada. In the. main, sir, considering the present financial stringency and economic depression in every province of Canada, I think we may be exceedingly fortunate if we are able to maintain the freight rate structure on its present basis, remembering the tremendous railway problem confronting us as a nation. At the same time, if there is to be a general increase in freight rates in order to keep our railways in existence, I do not know that the Canadian people would object so very much, but I do think that every intelligent opinion is properly directed against inequality as between one section and another with regard to the freight rate structure. For a number of years our people in British Columbia, have felt this differential very keenly; as I said last year, it is a matter of life and death to the poultry raisers and the dairymen of the Fraser valley, so we on this side appreciate the very fair and conciliatory attitude of the Minister of Railways this evening.
May I further point out to my hon. friend that the decision given in August, 1927, by the Board of Railway Commissioners, on the application made in 1926, was not submitted to the previous administration until September, 1929. In that appeal were joined together the provinces of British Columbia, 
Alberta and Saskatchewan, and at the request of the provinces the appeal was postponed until January of 1930. The session of that year, as those who were here will recall, opened on February 7, so the very consideration adduced by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister during the debate a year ago, that the government could not be expected to hear the appeal while parliament was in session, applied with equal force during the session of 1930. Immediately after that we had an appeal to the country, with all the tumult and turmoil of a general election. So I do not think, sir, any undue blame can be attached to the old administration for being dilatory in hearing this appeal.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, I addressed a request to the Prime Minister, which was referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for New Westminster. My request was for an assurance that after the session was terminated this appeal would be heard without undue delay. That assurance was given and will be found at page 1795 of Hansard for last year. Tonight my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has repeated that assurance, and with that assurance I suppose the house must rest content. I think hon. gentlemen opposite will find us on this side fair minded in supporting action along this line. There are two great issues to be considered; there is the question of assisting a wonderful body of people, some of the finest citizens in Canada, and there is also the larger national issue which is now under review by a great quasi-judicial tribunal, so while we are awaiting their decision perhaps this particular question is not possible of immediate solution,

Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to agree to a very large extent with the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) when he says that in general rate making is a question for the Board of Railway Commissioners. Whether we get the best results from them or not, the fact is that in the main parliament has entrusted to their hands the question of rate making. On August 26, 1927, they came to a conclusion with regard to a portion if not all of this particular resolution, from which decision the three western provinces and the United Farmers of British Columbia, whose headquarters are in the Fraser river valley, have appealed. That appeal has not been brought on for hearing since the present government took office, and if the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) will dig into the facts with regard to the delay in the hearing,
I think he will find that the federal government is not very much to blame with regard to the matter. The hearing before the previous government took place in part in the fall of 1929. The final argument before the previous government was not in the latter part of January, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) stated. Of course he wanted to get fairly close to the time when the session met. To be exact, the final argument took place on the 16th and 17th of January, 1930. No decision, however, was reached.
While I say I am in agreement to quite an extent with the contention that rate making should be in the hands of 'the Board of Railway Commissioners, nevertheless parliament has two functions. It has a legislative function whereby it can, if it so desires pass legislation which ties the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That was done in the session of 1925 with respect to the question of the Crowsnest rates on grain and flour moving eastward, and by order in council P.C. 886 it was directed that freight rates eastward and westward should be equalized. That was why the export rate to Vancouver was reduced to 20 cents. But while parliament has a legislative function, it has also an educative

function. Surely parliament should at least lead public opinion. Public opinion is to some extent moulded by the debates which take place in this house, and public opinion has an effect upon railways.
I listened with much interest to the figures given this afternoon by the Minister of Railways and Canals, but I confess that I have not as much confidence in figures supplied by the railway companies as I once had. At one time it was stated on no less an authority than Sir Henry Thornton that wheat could be shipped by barge from the Canadian National Railways terminal on the western coast to Victoria for not more than 88 per carload. Application was made to the Board of Railway Commissioners that the Canadian Pacific Railway be ordered to provide a rate from Victoria to Vancouver, and this company, through the use of the amazing experts it has to figure out costs, succeeded in proving to the commission that it could not be done for less than $30 per car. I think something like that must have occurred when they figured out the domestic rate from Edmonton to the coast at 41 cents, and claimed that that was the lowest possible rate which could be maintained.
The poultry and cattle industries on the lower Vancouver mainland and on Vancouver island are very important. The pouitryman in British Columbia must compete with the pouitryman in the Montreal district. During a hearing before the Board of Railway Commissioners on various points, one of -the railway commissioners stated that the consumer of grain and fl-our in Vancouver, and the dairy farmer, -the live stock feeder and the poultry-man in the territory contiguous to Vancouver, pay 372 per cent more than the consumer of grain and flour in Montreal, or the dairy farmer, the live stock feeder and the poultry-man in the territory contiguous to Montreal, in transportation costs on grain and flour produced in western Canada. The distance from Fort William to Montreal is 997 miles while the distance from Calgary to Vancouver is only 642. The western pouitryman is therefore under a considerable handicap as compared with his Montreal competitor, and possibly something should be done. However, if the reduction of this rate is going to cause a tremendous loss to -the railroads; if it means *that either the railroad -companies -or the poultrymen on the lower Vancouver mainland will have -to go under, I would prefer to save the railroads.
The arguments now being used against this reduction were used in 1927, 1928 and 1929 when the railroads were able to obtain plenty

Western Freight Rates
of freight. To-day transportation conditions are not as good, but if they improved the railroads would still use the same arguments. It is worthy of note that when the railroads chose to reduce their passenger rate between Ottawa and Montreal they increased vastly the traffic between those two cities. The traffic was there but it was not moving because the transportation cost was too high, but when the fare was reduced to a very marked extent the railroads were able to obtain many passengers and make more money than they had made at the higher rate. The consumer in British Columbia is obtaining his wheat and flour from Australia rather than from Alberta, in my opinion because the freight rates between Alberta and British Columbia are prohibitive. If the railroads could see their way clear to lower these rates to some extent they would induce traffic to move which would be much more advantageous than no traffic at all. The railroads might begin to make a little money instead of not making any. They have idle rolling stock, they have idle engines, they have idle men; the overhead still goes on but there is no traffic in grain and flour because the rate is prohibitive. If their costs are figured on the same basis as when the rolling stock was busy, they might have an argument, but I submit they would be much better off to be using their rolling stock than to allow it to stand idle and rust on the tracks. Other businesses find that it pays to keep their plants moving even if they make little or no profit.
If grain could move from the prairies to Vancouver and to Vancouver island there is no question that the live stock and poultry industries would be built up much more rapidly than is now the case. By giving these industries a chance to live the railroads would increase their traffic and as they increased their traffic they would increase their profits.
There is another point to be considered in connection with this reduction. This resolution asks that the domestic rate be substantially reduced while, if I remember aright, the resolution moved by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was of a different nature. This resolution covers more ground and is different in character. The hon. member's resolution suggested that the export and domestic rates on grain moving from the prairies to the coast should be the same, but that request is contrary to the desire of the three western provinces and the United Farmers of British Columbia. There is a reason for that. The export rate on wheat does not apply to wheat exported through Vancouver or Victoria to the United States; any wheat travelling through these points to
Seattle has to pay the domestic rate. If the domestic rate is made to equal the export rate it is feared that our hard wheat would then move to Seattle to be milled, exactly as it is moving to Buffalo. The result would be that the by-products from such milling would be available for American stock and not for the feeding of stock on Vancouver island and on the Vancouver lower mainland. We would then be assisting in building up competition in the United States against our own producers. Without our hard wheat the United States could not make a flour to compete with Canadian flour, yet we supply them at Buffalo with our wheat to enable them to make flour to undersell our flour on the markets of the world. We do not want a repetition of that on the Pacific coast, and for that reason the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan and the United Farmers of British Columbia, in the case they have laid before the governor in council, have asked that the domestic and export rates be not necessarily the same but be brought closer together, taking into consideration the desirability of maintaining the advantage of milling in Canada as against milling in the United States. There is a difference of opinion as to what the differential should be, but I do not think it is more than ten cents in any case. It is felt that if the domestic rate was reduced to 30 cents that differential would be ample to ensure the milling of our flour either at the coast or on the prairie provinces.
My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was a little astray with regard to what happened as to the first decision on domestic freight rates. That decision was afterwards rescinded. On September 2, 1925, there was a general order-in the middle of the election, one of my colleagues suggests-made by either two or three of the members of the Board of Railway Commissioners, equalizing freight rates east and west and equalizing, to some extent, the domestic and export rates; but in the meantime, after this had been referred to the board, only a part of whom had heard the application, another general order had been made by the government, this famous P.C. 886 in which a general inquiry into freight rates was ordered. Now as soon as the decision of September 2, 1925, was arrived at after a hearing by a part of the board, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company applied to the complete board to rescind the order, and on the application to rescind, as my hon. friend from New Westminster said, three members of the board were in favour of rescinding and three in favour of the order. But the application to rescind did not fail, as my hon. friend said, and the order of Septem-

Western Freight Rates

ber 2, 1925, was not confirmed, as my hon. friend said, but the six commissioners agreed that the matter would be reviewed again as a part of the general freight rate inquiry. That is what happened at that particular time.
When the general freight rate inquiry came on the decision was arrived at in the autumn of 1927. The united board dismissed the application to make the domestic rate the same as the export rate and left it at 41 cents per one hundred. It was from that decision that the present appeal was taken and is before the government at the present time.
There is one particular in which a lower rate would be of very great advantage to the northern parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan in particular-probably to southern Alberta more than to southern Saskatchewan and not so much to southern Alberta as to the northern part-and that is with regard to the movement westward of low grade grains, below contract grades. Owing to weather conditions the' north is likely to have a greater share of off-grade grains than the south, and the market for these grades, especially since mixing with the higher grades has been abolished, has become a difficult proposition. If there was some way of providing a special rate so that the low grade grains could be carried back and forth through the provinces and from northern Alberta to Vancouver and Vancouver island, it would be a great relief to the farmers of northern Alberta in particular, and to the feeders of grain in the southern part of British Columbia.
In connection with the rates on grain there is this to be observed. The present so-called Crowsnest rates on grain and flour are now statutory. They were statutory for many years as a matter of agreement between the railway and the crown, confirmed by statute, and maintained until suspended in 1919. That suspension was lifted in 1925, but instead of restoring the Crowsnest rates in toto the act, being chapter 52 of the statutes of 1925, gave the board the power to fix rates and enforce a reasonable I'ate structure. That abrogated the Crowsnest pass agreement and the Crowsnest pass rates. The Crowsnest pass agreement covered some twelve different articles, and by that act of 1925, while we did succeed in getting the Crowsnest pass rates on grain and flour established as maximum rates on those two commodities, we lost the benefit of the Crowsnest pass agreement on every one of the ten other commodities covered in the agreement. If my hon. friends opposite would examine the effect of that on the price of farm machinery and the price of lumber in western Canada, they would be doing a much better service to their constituents than by

trying to make out that reductions in the tariff in farm machinery have reduced the price, because the price of farm machinery was never reduced by the Liberal government during all the years between 1921 and 1930. In fact the price of farm machinery was higher in Canada the day they went out of office than the day they came in, in spite of the fact that the tariff was reduced and in spite of the fact that the whole sales tax was taken off -and maybe because of that fact rather than in spite of it.
I might remind the members of the house, Mr. Speaker, that the west has not entirely forgotten that they have lost the benefit of the Crowsnest pass agreement on everything but grain and flour, and some day when times are a little better and the railways, under the direction and guidance of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, become more prosperous than they are at the present moment, we are coming back to the board to see what we can do in that regard.

The west is under particular difficulties in regard to freight rates, particularly my own part of the country. I have watched the freight rate structure for some years, and rightly or wrongly I have come to the conclusion that there is an underlying principle with regard to the fixing of freight rates. The principle I saw established in regard to freight rates was the principle first established by the railways themselves, and confirmed more or less by the Board of Railway Commissioners as applied to the rates in force when the board was appointed. As I see it, the idea of the railways was to move the farm products of western Canada into eastern markets at as low a rate as they reasonably could, and as a result the freight rates on farm products travelling eastward were lower than the freight rates on farm products travelling westward. I do not know how that affected the maritime provinces. On the other hand, the rates westward on manufactured goods and building materials were lower than the rates eastward, and to-day manufactured goods can still be shipped westward more cheaply than eastward, which is a great handicap to the development of the manufacturing industry in western Canada. On those principles the railway rates were established. Then when my hon. friend the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) attempted to establish a port at Vancouver and have an elevator built at Vancouver harbour, which my hon. friends for many years called "Stevens' folly," the fight began to get a freight rate which would make it possible to move the grain westward to Vancouver. That is where the fight for an equalization of freight rates westward began. That fight has continued down to the present day with some success, but perhaps not with success as complete as it might have been. We have still the mountain- differential to fight with; there is the difference of 15 per cent. I think the Board of Railway Commissioners have found that freight can be moved west as cheaply as it can be moved east. There are still more than 120 miles to pay for which do not exist between Calgary and Vancouver owing to the longer haul between Edmonton and Vancouver. All these years, since there has been a harbour at Vancouver, the battle has been on to secure an equalization of freight rates westward. It has been conducted mostly in the interests of the elevator companies and 41761-56 i
the farmers who sold wheat to elevator companies for export. The result of the battle has been that export rates from time to time have been reduced by the railway commissioners, either under direction of parliament, or without direction of that body. However, the domestic movement was comparatively small, and while the export movement was reduced the domestic remained stationary at the old high level which was established before the Board of Railway Commissioners came into being. That to my mind is the reason-and I am speaking more in argument than from figures-why there is such a spread between export and domestic rates from Alberta to the Pacific coast. While that may be a matter for the Board of Railway Commissioners to decide, the fact is that that body has made a decision, and has decided against any reduction in domestic freight rates west. So that if the governor in council, when this matter comes before them, decide to refer it back to the Board of Railway Commissioners, they will be faced with the necessity of sending it back with some direction, because since the board has already decided against the western provinces there is very little use sending it back to them to make a further decision unless some direction is given that they decide more favourably than they did the last time.
There seems to be evidence to show that it is in the interests of the country that such action be taken. After all there have been occasions in days gone by when parliament exercised that right, when they found it in the interests of the people generally to lay down a policy for the Board of Railway Commissioners to follow; because after all parliament is supreme. It could direct by statute that the Board of Railway Commissioners follow certain principles. If parliament chose to say to the Board of Railway Commissioners that in the opinion of hon. members assembled, domestic freight rates are too high, and that in the interests of the Dominion of Canada and of the railways that rate could be reduced, although I am not an experienced parliamentarian, my own poor opinion would be that parliament would be justified in laying down such legislation. I am not saying such a right is one which should be exercised on all occasions; it should be exercised only with the greatest hesitation and the greatest care, because after all, the striking of freight rates is a very intricate problem. It is a matter to be settled not by a court of 245 persons, but rather, as the Minister of Railways has said, by a very much smaller court which could have the advantage of hearing both sides of the question.
Western Freight Rates

For the life of me I cannot understand why the domestic freight rate cannot be lowered to the advantage of both the railway companies and the industries in the Fraser valley to which my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) is so partial. In addition the industries on Vancouver island, to which he has not made reference, would benefit, as would the farmers in the prairie provinces. I am told that every week about 300 empty railroad cars are carried from the mainland to Vancouver island, and that in those cars products of Vancouver island are brought back to the mainland. I cannot see why the railroads would be under any great expense if they were to put wheat in those cars; it could be taken to Vancouver Maud with very little added cost. If such traffic were encouraged it would become extensive enough so that the cars might be taken over full instead of empty. It seems to me that if the matter is properly put before the railway companies-as I hope it will be-in the course of time, with public opinion behind us, we may reach a solution satisfactory to all concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this discussion, until I heard the remarks of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull). First of all may I deal with the statements made by the hon. member for Regina to the effect that the resolution now under discussion proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) is entirely different from that proposed by my good friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid). May I be permitted to read the resolution as presented by the hon. member for New Westminster:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the freight rates on grain and grain products destined to points in British Columbia from the prairie provinces of Canada be carried by the railways at the same rate as grain and grain products for export to other countries.
May I say to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, however, that I am really more pleased to support his motion. What does it say?
That, in the opinion of this house, the domestic freight rate on grain and grain products moving from any point in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, to a point in any of the said provinces, or from one point to another point in any one of the said provinces, be substantially reduced.
I think those of us who are farming in any of the four western provinces will receive greater benefit from the resolution presented by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle than from the one presented by the hon. member for

New Westminster. Under that resolution it would be possible for a farmer in the northern part of Saskatchewan to ship low grade wheat, or any wheat for that matter, to the southern part of the province, and receive the export rate thereon. I am all for it.
The Minister of Railways made comparisons of the rates on other commodities moving in Canada, both for domestic and export purposes. Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this resolution has been presented in such detail and with such a wealth of argument by the mover and those who have spoken in his support as to render it unnecessary for me to deal with it other than briefly. It is, however, I think extremely desirable that someone from the province of Alberta should at least express an opinion, and a very decided opinion, as representing the sentiments of that province.
As has been stated by other speakers, this matter in its present or a somewhat similar form has been before the house for some eight or ten years. During all that time this grievance, as we term it, has existed, not always in the same proportions as now, but still it has existed, and I believe that almost every session during that period although it has been very fully discussed nothing has been done. In a word, the situation has remained unchanged.
As I have intimated, it is not my purpose to go into the subject fully, but it does appear to'me that we are in a very anomalous position at the present time. Under our national policies as a parliament and as a government we are doing what we can to encourage not international and foreign trade only, but to develop domestic and interprovincial trade to the greatest possible degree. I am fully in favour of developing to the maximum trade between the component parts of Canada. There are no two parts of the Dominion that offer greater opportunities for an interchange that will be mutually beneficial than do the province of British Columbia on the one hand and the prairie provinces on the other. I have always felt that my own province in particular, Alberta, and the province of British Columbia are complementary and supplementary one to the other to a very marked degree, and that they should to a far greater extent than has been the case during the past years go forward side by side working together in their mutual interest. In this case it is a very great pleasure to me, as it has been to many others in the house, to find a subject upon which we may agree so fully and an end towards which we can work in such complete harmony.
The situation has been laid before the house, a situation under which thousands of fanners within the British Columbia valleys, where the climate and soil are admirably adapted to the most intensive forms of poultry raising, dairy farming and other kindred forms of agriculture,, find themselves completely handicapped through the fact that although grown only a few hundred miles away the products of the great grain fields of the prairie provinces are almost inaccessible to them, that they are shut out from the use of those products by a wall greater far as barrier than distance, by a wall more exclusive than oceans and continents, by a wall erected in a wholly arbitrary fashion-a wall of excessive freight rates. On the other hand, the farmers of the prairie provinces, looking westward as their shortest and cheapest route to the markets of Europe and to the great and developing trade in the orient which they visualize as their most hopeful market in the future, are also looking closer home across those mountain barriers beyond which they see thousands of potential and would-be	customers-customers anxious to
purchase their grain products and to exchange their own in return.
This is a situation which I think should not be beyond the intelligence and ability of this house and this government to rectify. It has been stated by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion)-and in a general way I am in agreement with him-that by reason of the characteristics of their make-up neither the house nor the government is the best possible court for deciding a question so technical in its nature as that of freight rates. But on the other hand I conceive that this parliament must be responsible at least for one thing-for the laying down of national policies, and that within the lines of those policies all commissions of a technical character must function. I submit that parliament itself cannot delegate to any other body, especially a body that is not responsible directly to the people, the right to determine what policies shall be followed-policies for which parliament itself must be responsible. As I see it, we confer upon the railway commission power, not to lay down policies for this country, but within the limits set by parliament to look after the details of which the minister spoke. And when we deal with matters of internal trade, matters which must affect intimately the wellbeing and livelihood of the people of two or more provinces, then we enter a field which is too large to be left wholly to the railway commission or to any other body which we may constitute.
Western Freight Rates

Possibly it is true that the right of appeal to the privy council from decisions of the railway commission should not continue, that such appeals should be heard by the supreme court, the exchequer court or some other tribunal. But so long as the present law continues in force that responsibility rests on the government, and until the law is abrogated that responsibility cannot be evaded by the government. I am not going into the question now as to whether undue delay has taken place on the part of this government or its predecessors. I do suggest, however, that sufficient time has elapsed and that now we may well look to the government for action of one kind or another. Whether it be in the form of a reference back to the railway commission with instructions as to the lines within which they should work and the goal towards which they should strive, or in the direction of designating some other and perhaps more suitable body to do this work, in any case let us put an end to this period of suspense and indicate to the farmers and the other citizens of the provinces interested that within a reasonable time this disability shall as far as possible be removed, and those necessary goods shall go on backward and forward at the least possible cost.
It has been argued, and perhaps with some truth, that the Canadian Pacific Railway faces certain definite geographical handicaps, that it has a heavy mountain grade and that it cannot be reasonably expected to haul tonnage over the mountains at anything like a prairie rate. It might also be said, and has been said, it would be totally unfair to use the comparatively low and easy grade of the Canadian National railways as a weapon with which to coerce the other system. But, Mr. Speaker, let us go back a few years, comparatively speaking, and what do we find? We find that the Canadian Pacific Railway, being first in the field, had ample opportunity and a perfect right to have chosen that low grade had it so desired, but at that time those directing the Canadian Pacific Railway did not see, nor could very many men foretell, the tremendous movement of freight westward which might develop. So, not foreseeing that great movement, their actions would indicate that they naturally expected the factor to which they must look for their greatest profit to be the passenger traffic and, by providing a scenic route over and through our beautiful mountains, they exepected to attract a great tourist traffic and provide themselves with ample profit. Possibly they were quite justified in figuring it in that way, but is it right that the citizens of these
(Mr. Speakman.]
provinces should be compelled forever to pay scenic freight rates because, forsooth, thirty or forty years ago the Canadian Pacific built a scenic railway in order to attract tourist traffic? Is it right that we should be forever debarred from the advantages which would naturally accrue from the easy grades which the Canadian National railway now follows? It has been proved and demonstrated, so amply and so frequently as to require no repetition, that following the line of the Canadian National railway westward we find grades that compare favourably with those found in the movement eastward, so the mountain differential is a fantasy, a mere dream, a figment of the imagination, with no actuality in fact. There is no such thing as a mountain grade or a mountain range when going through the Yellowhead pass. Most of us have travelled over that road and we have seen for ourselves. We have seen the number of freight cars a locomotive will haul both east and west, and perhaps it is not necessary to assure you, Mr. Speaker, or to indicate to any hon. member of the house, that the power used to haul a train of cars from the prairies to Fort William is sufficient to haul at least an equal tonnage through the mountain passes.
Under those circumstances, and in view of the fact that our present policies encourage the development of domestic and interprovincial rather than international trade, to a greater degree than ever before it is imperative that we should take action in this matter and make it possible for that interprovincial trade to proceed. It does seem to me that a curious paradox exists. By means of subsidies and tariffs and every possible policy within the grasp of the government of this country we have done our best to encourage this trade as between provinces, and the paradox is that we should longer tolerate a freight rate structure which is indefensible under any circumstances-indeed which no one has endeavoured to defend, except to say that it is necessary to find from some source profits which are not obtained elsewhere. So it is that we compel those who wish to ship their grain within the country to pay for a loss which has been sustained on another part of the system. That is the only argument I have heard, and that argument cannot be sustained morally or logically.
In view of these facts I repeat that this house should indicate its desire to have something done. I was glad to hear the sympathetic expressions which emanated from the Minister of Railways, and I think we should indicate to the railway commission that, leav-

Western Freight Rates
ing to them the settlement of those matters of detail which are within their province, public policy and public necessity alike demand that this matter should be reconsidered in the light of the greatest good to the greatest number, in the light of justice and common sense, and that this curious, archaic anomaly of freight rates should not longer exist. The Minister of Railways said he could discover no specific basis upon which our freight rate structure was built; to a layman like myself, and I may be pardoned for saying in some degree like himself, it is a confused patchwork of rates apparently based on some factor with which we are not acquainted; thrown together, complicated and so complex in its nature that we cannot properly comprehend it. That may be true, Mr. Speaker, but we can comprehend this particular item; we can see here something which should not exist, and therefore I repeat that parliament and the government should indicate very clearly to those charged with the immediate responsibility that this state of affairs must not continue, that they must so arrange our rates that they shall no longer act as an effective barrier against natural interprovincial trade and the proper future development of the western provinces.

The hon. member for Regina sought to make a point by urging that those on this side of the house should have remembered that certain things were omitted from the Crowsnest pass agreement when it was restored, instead of giving our attention to reductions in tariff. Perhaps I might briefly review the facts in that regard, and I think I will state those facts in such a way that no person will dispute them.
As the 'hon. member pointed out, that agreement was suspended in 1919, and the suspension lapsed on July 8, 1922. For the three years following that, the whole matter was in a somewhat unsettled condition, being discussed by the Board of Railway Commissioners and the courts. I need not go into that. But in the session of 1925 the government of the day brought in a resolution restoring in part
the Crowsnest pass agreement. If that were the whole story, we might even claim that half a loaf was better than no bread. If the Conservatives of that day had had their way, we would not have had even half a loaf, for during all the discussion from 1921 onward the whole force of the Conservative party in this parliament was arrayed against the restoration of the Crowsnest pass rates. No person will dispute that statement, for Hansard will show it. But I say, when we make that statement we have not told the whole story. The agreement was only partly restored. The contention had been raised that the agreement applied only to that part of the Canadian Pacific railway which was in existence when the original agreement was made. So, when this bill was brought down in 1925 by the government of the day, it is true it abrogated the rates on goods moving west, but it made it clear that the rates on grain and grain products applied not only to that portion of the Canadian Pacific railway which was in existence when the agreement was originally made, but to the whole Canadian Pacific system and to the Canadian National system as well. Well, the Votes and Proceedings will bear out something very different. If the hon. member will take the trouble to refer to the Votes and Proceedings of that date, he will find there a different story entirely. He says that the government of that day brought in a measure restoring in part the Crowsnest pass agreement. It was not necessary for the then government to bring in a bill to restore that agreement; all the government had to do was to sit still and let the agreement go back into force. The hon. member for Lisgar knows that. He ought to know, if he does not, that a committee was appointed, at the instance of the government, to consider the matter. That committee consisted of Conservatives, Liberals and Progressives, the Liberals having more on it than either of the other parties in the house, and the Progressives being the next largest group. In that committee a resolution was proposed to allow the Crowsnest pass agreement to go back into force in its entirety. The committee was equally divided on the resolution

and the Liberal chairman gave his casting vote that the agreement should not go back into effect in its entirety. That is borne out by the Votes and Proceedings and everyone in the house is aware of the fact. Yet the Liberals will go throughout the country telling the people: We restored the Crowsnest pass agreement. It did not need any restoration at all; all the then government had to do was to sit still and let it go back into force.
The matter of freight rates is very intricate, and when a layman who has no knowledge of railroading attempts to deal with it, he is naturally going to be met with the statement that "Fools rush in where angels fear to tread." There is a good deal of justification for that statement as regards the question of dealing with freight rates. Therefore I do not propose to deal with the scientific side of freight rates or to question the arguments put forward by the railway companies, as I do not feel I am in a position to do so. But in connection with freight rates I wish to point out some things that I think might be considered.
We are told in this world to accept things as facts when in reality they are only theories. To illustrate what I mean, when the steam engine was first proposed as a motive power for transportation, the people of England appointed a commission to inquire into the feasibility of using steam on railways for transportation purposes. That commission consisted of very able men, and hon. members might be astonished to know that its report read something like this: that steam as a motive power in transportation might be of some value particularly in the matter of transporting freight, but for anyone to suggest that the travelling public would trust themselves in a railway carriage drawn by a steam locomotive at the ridiculous rate of fifteen miles an hour, was absurd; such a thing would never take place. How far astray that theory was, time has amply proven.
There is another illustration that is perhaps even a little more in point. There was a time when it was believed that penny postage was the most absurd thing in the world. Why, the idea of carrying a letter for two cents was unthinkable! But when penny postage was introduced the volume of mail handled increased at such a rate that after all the post office returns were better at the two cent rate than they had been at the ridiculously high rates formerly charged. When you start to apply that principle to the question of freight rates, in order to be fair to the railways and to everybody else you must acknowledge that another factor enters into the question: that is, that we are living

in a country some four thousand miles in extent and a great deal of it very sparsely populated. The question naturally arises: Even if those rates were reduced very materially, is it possible to develop sufficient business? Is sufficient business there, or can it be brought there to make those rates pay? The railways tell us that they have investigated this matter and that their experts tell them it is impossible to make those rates pay; that the business is not there, nor can it be developed. But again I say to the railways: that is, after all, a matter of theory, because it has never been tried. The only way to demonstrate whether, on a reduction of freight rates, sufficient business will develop to make the railways pay on those reduced rates, is to make the experiment. Until that is done we are acting entirely on a basis of theory. I am not prepared even to say that my opinion is that the railways could be made to pay better on that very much reduced rate, but it would be a very useful experiment, and if it should work out, it would be like the penny postage, a great blessing to humanity. We must not presume simply because this theory has stood for so many years that it is a fact. After all it is only a theory.
The question arises as to why the government is not dealing with this. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), who is always very clear and moderate in his statements, has suggested that it is time the government did something. This appeal, however, was brought by the provinces and I do not think they are at the present time very anxious to have it heard. That perhaps is the reason why the government has been unable to get them together. They may not have stated frankly the reason, but I think they do not consider this an opportune time to have the appeal heard. How the government is going to bring the appeal on unless the provinces come forward with their case is something I do not know. The Prime Minister (Mr Bennett) stated that a date was set, but that the provinces stated they were not ready to go on; consequently the appeal was not heard. As the hon. member for Regina has said, unless the government is prepared to give some direction or offer some suggestion there is little advantage to be gained simply by hearing the appeal and sending it back to the railway commission to be retried. That body decided on the evidence placed before it and without a specific direction no doubt would decide again in the same manner.
I think everyone agrees that the railways are in a very difficult position, and it is well

Western Freight Rates
known that the people of this country are carrying a great burden in that connection. Any government which attempts to deal with this situation as far as the western provinces are concerned is faced with a very serious problem. I doubt very much if there are many people who, after having this question explained, would be prepared to suggest to the government that it adopt a definite course one way or another. It will be said, of course, that the people are looking to the government for a lead, but I think they can rest assured that the government will take definite steps in this respect. That the rates are entirely out of line would seem evident from the fact that goods can be shipped from Calgary to the orient at a lower rate than they can be shipped to Vancouver.
If I had any objection to the resolution it would be that it does not go far enough. The people in British Columbia grow some splendid fruit which is needed badly in the western provinces. There are occasions when we in the western provinces are hungry for fruit which is rotting in the orchards of British Columbia. Perhaps the railroads will take it into their heads to try the experiment which they have made in the passenger rates between Montreal and Ottawa. However, there is this difficulty: you cannot develop freight over night; it would take some little time and the railroads might get weary of well doing before the results of the reduction in rates would be felt. That the railroads are facing a serious problem I think is apparent to every hon. member in this house. The one encouraging feature of this debate is the fact that hon. members on both sides have recognized the necessity of protecting the railroads to the extent of allowing them to charge a fair rate in order that they may keep going and serve the people of this great country.
I am heartily in favour of the resolution, but I would like to see it go a little further so that we could get the products of British Columbia into the prairie provinces. I am not an expert in freight rates and I am not prepared to say what should be done, but I certainly would like to see an experiment made to test the old theory that a reduction in rates will not produce a sufficient increase in business to justify its being put into effect.

I do not see the necessity-nor has this ever been asked, except by resolution-for making the domestic and the export rates comparable, but there should be some paring down of the domestic rates on grain to bring them more in line with the export rates.
I do not intend to traverse the whole field, but may I say that in my opinion parliament is totally unfitted to deal with a matter of this kind. We may express an opinion, but we have not the time or the opportunity to obtain full information with respect to all aspects of the question. May I carry that point a little further and say that despite the fact that it has had an opportunity of hearing both sides of the question discussed, despite the fact that new matter has been interjected into the discussion, the government must find itself in a very difficult position in coming 'to a decision upon a question as involved as this. I have had the privilege of listening to two or three appeals from the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I am firmly convinced that the government should not be a court of appeal. A question of this kind should be submitted either to the supreme court or to the exchequer court. Coming to a conclusion in connection with freight rates is most difficult; both sides of the question are advanced so strongly, precedents have to be considered, and then there is a possibility of that happening which has happened to-day-a continued extension and widening out of the circle of the application until you finally reach the stage where you do not feel like taking the responsibility of a decision. There must be considered the possibility of jeopardizing the interests of the railroads, one of which is a national undertaking, and of necessity entitled to some protection from the government.

It is very difficult, therefore, for a government to come to a decision upon a question so involved as that of freight rates. I think I am safe in stating that during the time the Liberal party was in office we followed the practice of returning these questions to the railway commission for consideration. Something of that kind could be done with this matter. The commissioners could be instructed to give consideration to the question of the differential between the export and domestic rates on grain going to British Columbia, and I am not unmindful of the fact that perhaps something might be done to solve the problem facing the maritime provinces.
These two questions are similar in every particular. Products are going to the ports of export and in no way do they interfere with the internal rates either in the maritimes, in Quebec and Ontario or the iprairie provinces. I.f these two questions were out of the way and some readjustment made, I think it would go a long way towards the settling of this vexed question which has been agitating the mind of parliament and particularly of the people of Alberta and British Columbia. May I say here and now that I think the government would be wise, if appeals are to be allowed to have the act amended, to have at the earliest possible date those appeals go to the supreme court or the exchequer court.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the suggestions made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) with regard to the responsibility or jurisdiction of parliament in a matter of this character. For parliament as a body to attempt to adjust freight rates or to go into all the details in connection with freight rates is entirely out of the question. My opinion is that for the government itself to act as a court of appeal to hear cases coming from the railway commission and to go into the details of freight rates is also out of the question. But freight rates being what they are, applying as they do to all commodities in Canada that must be transported, often considerable distances, and being so intimately linked up with our export trade, being in a word one of the most important factors affecting the Canadian people, I believe it would be well for parliament to lay down a principle that should apply in determining the differential between the export and domestic rates in all parts of Canada. I might stand here and cite case after case, not so exaggerated perhaps as those that have been cited as between the prairie provinces and Vancouver,

but nevertheless showing a very wide spread between the domestic and export rates which it is difficult to understand. It is indeed difficult to understand sometimes why domestic business is penalized as it is, but the problem that must be dealt with is this: the railways must have revenue, and we must treat all classes of industry fairly. We cannot select a particular commodity or a particular locality and apply a principle with respect to it that should not be applied to every other commodity and in every other part of Canada. Having given the matter such consideration as it can give in a debate of this character, and having ascertained the general view of the country in regard to the subject, parliament might well appoint a committee to study the question and hear interested parties in all parts of Canada, with a view to laying down the principle that should be followed in determining the extent of the differential between the export and domestic rates and between the short-haul and long-haul rates. In that way something might be accomplished; but simply to throw the question back to the railway commission without instructions is to invite a decision similar to the one already given.
I do not agree with my hon. friend the exMinister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), who has just spoken, that these questions should be settled one at a time, because when you deal with one particular commodity or one particular locality, you cannot help but discriminate against some other commodity or some other locality. If the railways are to get sufficient revenue to make it possible for them to continue to operate, when the freight rate is reduced on one commodity moving from one particular point to another, it must perhaps be raised on some other commodity, and you are simply taking the burden from one industry and placing it on another. The problem is so vast, the details are so innumerable, the range of country is so wide, the number of commodities that have to be transported is so large, that the question can be adequately dealt with only after an intensive study of all industries and after hearing all interested parties. But the subject might be referred to a committee of this house to report back the principle it thinks should be followed in determining what the differential, if any, should be.
It must also be borne in mind that one of our tremendous problems is to get our export products, particularly of the west, into the world markets on a basis that will enable them to compete. There are many commodities-lumber, for instance, newsprint, pulp, coal in the east and the west-vital to different

parts of this country, and in my opinion the only way in which the sense of parliament and of the people can be ascertained is by having the whole subject carefully inquired into by some body which will hear evidence from all parts of Canada and from all classes of people interested. It can then be determined whether it is the general desire to have the differential narrowed, and a principle can be laid down which will guide the commission in working out the details and reaching its decisions.
